questionText: Weather and Climate: Weather is the short-term atmospheric condition of a place, while climate is the average weather over a long period for a larger area. Weather changes frequently and is experienced over small areas; climate is more stable and covers larger regions.
mnemonic_hint: Weather is what you get today (short-term), Climate is what you expect over years (long-term).

questionText: Big Bang Theory: The universe originated from a tiny, dense, hot "ball" that exploded 13.7 billion years ago. The universe has been expanding since, with atoms forming within minutes and atomic matter appearing within 300,000 years as the universe cooled.
sub_topic: Origin and Evolution of the Universe
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'B-A-T': Big Bang, Atoms formed in minutes, Temperature cooled for matter.

questionText: Evolution of Atmosphere: Earth’s original hydrogen-helium atmosphere was lost to space due to solar winds. Volcanic activity released heavier gases, forming a secondary atmosphere. Photosynthetic organisms later produced oxygen, leading to today’s oxygen-rich atmosphere.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'H-V-O': Hydrogen lost, Volcanic gases rose, Oxygen grew.

questionText: Earth’s Habitability: Earth is in the Sun’s habitable zone, allowing liquid water. Its mass and gravity retain an atmosphere. The magnetic field shields the planet from harmful solar radiation, making Earth suitable for life.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'G-A-M': Goldilocks zone (water), Atmosphere (gravity), and Magnetic shield (protection).

questionText: Earth’s Layers: The crust (Sial—silica and aluminum), mantle (Sima—silica and magnesium), and core (Nife—nickel and iron) are Earth’s main layers. Sial forms continents, Sima provides magma, and Nife is dense and magnetic.
concepts: Density and magnetic properties of the core
mnemonic_hint: Remember the layers by their chemical initials: Sial (Si+Al), Sima (Si+Ma), and Nife (Ni+Fe).

questionText: Terrestrial and Jovian Planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are rocky terrestrial planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are gaseous Jovian planets with thick atmospheres and no solid surface.
sub_topic: Classification of Planets in the Solar System
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'MVEM' (My Very Earthly Mars) for the rocky inner planets, and 'JSUN' for the gaseous outer giants.

questionText: Rock Cycle: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks transform through geological processes. Sedimentary rocks form by lithification of fragments; igneous rocks form from cooled magma; metamorphic rocks form under heat and pressure.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SIM': Sedimentary (lithification), Igneous (magma), Metamorphic (heat/pressure).

questionText: Sedimentary Rocks: Clastic sedimentary rocks are made of cemented fragments from pre-existing rocks. Non-clastic (chemical) sedimentary rocks form from minerals precipitated from water, like limestone and chert.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'C-C' for Clastic-Cemented and 'C-P' for Chemical-Precipitated.

questionText: Diastrophism: Earth’s crust is shaped by orogenic (mountain-building), epeirogenic (uplift/warping), earthquakes, and plate tectonics. These processes cause folding, faulting, and metamorphism.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'O-E-E-P': Orogenic (Mountains), Epeirogenic (Elevation/Warping), Earthquakes, and Plate tectonics.

questionText: River Stages: Youthful rivers create V-shaped valleys and waterfalls; mature rivers have wider valleys and floodplains; old rivers meander over broad floodplains with oxbow lakes and natural levees.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Y-M-O': Youth cuts V-valleys, Mature makes plains, Old creates Oxbows.

questionText: Seismic Waves: Earthquakes generate body (P and S) and surface waves. P waves travel fastest through solids, liquids, and gases; S waves travel only through solids; surface waves are slowest.
mnemonic_hint: P-waves are 'Primary' (fastest/all media), S-waves are 'Secondary' (solids only), and Surface waves are 'Slowest' (surface only).

questionText: Plate Boundaries: Divergent boundaries create new crust (mid-ocean ridges), convergent boundaries destroy crust (subduction, mountain-building), and transform boundaries slide past each other without creating or destroying crust.
mnemonic_hint: Divergent creates (D-C), Convergent consumes (C-C), Transform travels (T-T) past.

questionText: Plateaus: Plateaus are flat uplands with steep sides. Intermontane plateaus are surrounded by mountains (e.g., Tibet), piedmont plateaus are at mountain bases (e.g., Malwa), and continental plateaus are uplifted or lava covered (e.g., Deccan).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'TIP': Tibet is Intermontane, Piedmont is Malwa, and Deccan is Continental.

questionText: Continental Drift Evidence: Matching continental shapes, similar rocks and fossils across oceans, placer deposits, and fossil distributions support the idea that continents were once joined and have drifted apart.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'F-R-O-P': Fossils, Rocks, Ocean-fit, and Placer deposits are the four pillars of drift evidence.

questionText: Abyssal Plains: Abyssal plains are flat, deep-sea floors covered by sediments (oozes or red clay). They lie between continental margins and mid-ocean ridges.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Abyssal' as 'A-Base-All'—the flat base covering the floor between the margins and the ridges.

questionText: Alluvial Fans and Bajadas: Alluvial fans form where rivers deposit sediments at mountain bases; bajadas are merged alluvial fans. They are common in arid regions and can also form by mass wasting (colluvial fans).
concepts: Deposition of sediments at mountain fronts
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Fan' spreading out at the base, and many 'Fans' joining together to form a 'Bajada' (like a 'Bazaar' of fans).

questionText: Solifluction: Slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil, common in moist temperate regions with seasonal thawing and prolonged rainfall.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Soil-Fluction' as soil flowing like a slow, thick liquid down a slope when saturated.

questionText: Erosional Processes: Erosion involves attrition (rock collision), hydraulic action (water pressure), deflation (wind removal of particles), abrasion (rock scraping), and corrosion (chemical dissolution).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CHAD-A': Corrosion, Hydraulic action, Attrition, Deflation, and Abrasion are the key erosional forces.

questionText: Igneous Rocks: Formed from solidified magma. Intrusive rocks cool slowly underground (large crystals, e.g., granite); plutonic rocks are deep-seated intrusive types.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Intrusive' as 'Inside' the earth, where slow cooling allows crystals to grow large like a giant (Granite).

questionText: Volcano Types: Composite volcanoes erupt viscous lava and pyroclastics; calderas form from explosive eruptions and collapse; flood basalt provinces (e.g., Deccan Traps) result from extensive lava flows.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'C-C-F': Composite is viscous/explosive, Calderas are collapsed, and Flood basalts are fluid/extensive.

questionText: Batholiths: Large, dome-shaped intrusive igneous bodies formed deep in the crust, often exposed after erosion, and form mountain cores.
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Bath'olith as a giant tub of magma cooling deep underground to form the 'bath' tub of a mountain.

questionText: Ring of Fire: A tectonically active zone encircling the Pacific Ocean, marked by frequent earthquakes and volcanoes. Includes Eurasian, North American, Juan de Fuca, Cocos, Nazca, and Philippine plates.
sub_topic: Plate Tectonics and Global Geological Features
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-E-N-C-J-N-P' for the plates: Pacific, Eurasian, North American, Cocos, Juan de Fuca, Nazca, and Philippine.

questionText: Indian Plate Boundaries: Includes Peninsular India and Australia; converges with Eurasia at the Himalayas, spreads east of Australia, and has divergent boundaries with the Antarctic plate.
mnemonic_hint: Think of the Indian plate as a 'H-E-A-D' collision: Himalayas (convergent with Eurasia), East (spreading), Antarctic (divergent).

questionText: Water Vapour: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in air, highest in warm tropics and lowest in cold/dry regions. Water vapour absorbs solar and terrestrial radiation, moderating Earth’s temperature.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'WET' (Water, Energy, Tropics): Water vapour is highest in the tropics and traps energy.

questionText: Air Pressure Distribution: Air pressure varies with temperature, rotation, and water vapour. Warm air and high humidity lower pressure; rotation creates pressure belts; isobars show pressure patterns.
concepts: Relationship between water vapour and air density
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-H-L': Warm air and High humidity lead to Low pressure.

questionText: Coriolis Force: An apparent force due to Earth’s rotation, deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern. Stronger at higher latitudes, zero at the equator.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Right-North' (RN) and 'Left-South' (LS) to recall the direction of deflection.

questionText: Atmospheric Heating: Four processes—conduction (contact), convection (vertical movement), radiation (energy transfer through space), and advection (horizontal movement)—transfer heat in the atmosphere.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CRAC': Conduction, Radiation, Advection, Convection—the four ways the atmosphere gets its 'crack' at heating up.

questionText: Jet Streams and Monsoons: Upper-level jet streams influence India’s climate. The westerly jet brings winter rain and hail to northwestern India via western disturbances.
mnemonic_hint: Westerly brings Winter: Think 'W-W' (Westerly-Winter) for the rain in the North-West.

questionText: Cloud Types: Cirrostratus (thin, halo), stratocumulus (patchy, not always dark), nimbostratus (thick, rain/snow), cumulus (vertical, fair weather). Clouds form when rising air cools and condenses.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CNCS' (Cirro, Nimbo, Cumulo, Strato) by thinking of 'Can New Clouds Stay' to recall the primary types.

questionText: Pressure Patterns in January: In January, low pressure occurs over hot land areas in the Southern Hemisphere; subtropical highs are over oceans, interrupted by warmer continents.
sub_topic: Global Pressure Belts and Seasonal Variations
concepts: Thermal contrast between land and sea
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Land is a Heat-Magnet': In summer, land heats up faster, creating low pressure, while oceans remain relatively cooler with high pressure.

questionText: Local Winds: Chinook (hot, dry, Rockies), Harmattan (hot, dry, West Africa), Zonda (warm, dry, Andes), Mistral (cold, dry, Alps to Mediterranean).
sub_topic: World Climatic Regions and Local Winds
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CHAMZ': Chinook (Rockies), Harmattan (Africa), Mistral (Alps), Zonda (Andes).

questionText: Mesosphere: The third atmospheric layer, up to 80 km, where temperature decreases with height and is the coldest part of the atmosphere; meteors burn up here.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Meso' as 'Meteor'—the layer where meteors meet their end.

questionText: Planetary Winds: Trade winds (easterlies) blow from subtropical highs to equatorial lows; polar easterlies blow from polar highs to subpolar lows; westerlies blow from subtropical highs to subpolar lows.
mnemonic_hint: Think of the 'W' in Westerlies as moving from the 'W'arm subtropical highs toward the poles.

questionText: Continental Margins: Include continental shelf (shallow, productive), slope (steep), rise (sediment accumulation), and deep-ocean trenches (deepest parts, near continents).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Shelf-Slope-Rise-Trench' as the 'SSR-T' sequence moving from the coast into the deep ocean.

questionText: Seafloor Spreading: New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges (active margins), moves away, and is eventually subducted or becomes part of passive margins (no subduction).
mnemonic_hint: Think of a conveyor belt: 'Rise at the ridge, ride away, and sink at the subduction zone.'

questionText: Ocean Temperature Profile: Surface ocean temperature averages 27°C, decreases with latitude and depth. Northern Hemisphere oceans are warmer due to more land; land heats/cools faster than water.
concepts: Differential Heating of Land and Water
mnemonic_hint: Think 'Land-Loves-Heat': Land heats and cools faster than water, making land-heavy Northern Hemisphere oceans warmer.

questionText: Ocean Currents and Climate: Warm currents (e.g., North Atlantic Drift) raise temperatures of nearby coasts; cold currents (e.g., Labrador) lower them. Currents affect coastal climates and ice conditions.
sub_topic: Ocean Currents and their Climatic Impact
concepts: Impact of warm and cold currents on coastal temperatures
mnemonic_hint: Warm currents bring the 'W' (Warmth) to the coast, while cold currents bring the 'C' (Chill) to the coast.

questionText: Seafloor Spreading Evidence: Youngest rocks at mid-ocean ridges, symmetrical magnetic stripes, and thin sediments support seafloor spreading; deep trenches have deep earthquakes, ridges have shallow ones.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'MARS': Magnetic stripes, Age increases away from ridge, Ridges are shallow, Sediments are thin.

questionText: Indian Ocean Currents: Northern Indian Ocean currents reverse with monsoons; southern part has anti-clockwise circulation like other oceans.
mnemonic_hint: Think of the Indian Ocean as a 'Seasonal Swing'—it flips its direction with the monsoon winds, unlike its steady southern neighbors.

questionText: Earth’s Crust Elements: Oxygen is the most abundant element by volume; silicon is second; aluminium is third by weight.
concepts: Elemental distribution by weight vs volume
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'OS Al' (Oh, Silly Aluminum) to recall the top three elements by weight in the crust: Oxygen, Silicon, and Aluminium.

questionText: Soil Properties: Soil consists of minerals, organic matter, air, and water. Dark soils have more organic matter, absorb more heat, and promote faster plant growth.
mnemonic_hint: Think of a dark shirt in the sun: Dark colors absorb more heat, just like dark, organic-rich soil.

questionText: Metamorphic Rocks: Formed from existing rocks under heat and pressure, are denser and harder, often foliated, and usually lack fossils.
sub_topic: Classification and Characteristics of Metamorphic Rocks
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'M-F-H': Metamorphic rocks are Formed by Heat/pressure and often show Foliation.

questionText: Karst Topography: Formed in limestone regions by groundwater solution, features include sinkholes, caves, and underground drainage; surface water is scarce.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'K-L-S': Karst is Limestone formed by Solution.

questionText: Sand Dunes: Barchans (crescent-shaped, one wind direction), transverse dunes (perpendicular to wind), seif/longitudinal dunes (parallel to wind), common in deserts.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'BTS': Barchans (Crescent), Transverse (Perpendicular), Seif (Parallel/Longitudinal).

questionText: Limestone Cave Features: Stalactites hang from ceilings, stalagmites rise from floors, both formed by calcium carbonate deposition; erosional features include sinkholes and lapies.
mnemonic_hint: Stalactites hold on 'tight' to the ceiling, while stalagmites 'might' reach the top one day.

questionText: Earth’s Mantle Layers: Upper and lower mantle separated by the Repetti Discontinuity; transition zone holds significant water; lithosphere and asthenosphere are upper mantle subdivisions.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'M-R-L' for Mantle-Repetti-Lower: Repetti sits between the upper and lower mantle.

questionText: Floodplains: Formed by river deposition during floods; natural levees are ridges along banks; point bars are deposits on meander bends.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'L-P-F': Levees are on the sides (banks), Point bars are on the bends, and Floodplains are the flat lands.

questionText: Delta Formation: Deltas form where rivers deposit sediments at their mouths; require active erosion, shallow and tideless seas, and sheltered coasts.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'STARS': Shallow, Tideless, Active erosion, River-sediment, Sheltered coast.

questionText: Glacial Landforms: Aretes (ridges), cols (passes), horns (pyramidal peaks), cirques (amphitheater-shaped hollows), crevasses (glacier cracks) are shaped by glacial erosion.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'HAC' (Horns, Aretes, Cirques) as the 'High Altitude Carvings' created by glacial ice.

questionText: Mountain Types: Fold mountains form by crustal compression (e.g., Himalayas); block mountains form by faulting (e.g., Vosges); horsts are uplifted blocks.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Fold' as a crumpled rug (compression) and 'Block' as a broken brick (faulting).

questionText: Mountain Formation: Residual mountains are erosion remnants (e.g., Scottish Highlands); volcanic mountains form from eruptions (e.g., Mauna Loa); dome mountains form from magma uplift.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'R-V-D': Residuals are Remnants, Volcanics are Vents, and Domes are Distended by magma.

questionText: Continental Drift Theory: Wegener proposed all continents were once joined as Pangaea, later split into Laurasia and Gondwanaland; evidence includes geology, fossils, and climate.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'PLG' for the sequence: Pangaea split into Laurasia (North) and Gondwanaland (South).

questionText: Major Minerals: Amphibole (asbestos, Rajasthan), quartz (hard, insoluble, Rajasthan), feldspar (ceramics, Rajasthan), mica (electrical, Andhra Pradesh).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'AR-QR-FR-MA': Asbestos-Rajasthan, Quartz-Rajasthan, Feldspar-Rajasthan, Mica-Andhra.

questionText: Wind Erosion: Wind shapes deserts through erosion (yardangs, blowouts) and deposition (loess, silt deposits).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Y-B-L' for wind: Yardangs and Blowouts are for erosion, Loess is for deposition.

questionText: Landslides: More frequent in the Himalayas due to tectonic activity, steep slopes, and weak geology; Western Ghats are older, more stable, and less prone.
mnemonic_hint: Himalayas are 'High' (Young/High activity), Western Ghats are 'Worn' (Old/Stable).

questionText: Pediments: Gently sloping rock surfaces at mountain bases in deserts, formed by erosion and retreat of slopes, leading to pediplains.
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Pediment' as a 'Foot-ment' (foot of the mountain) where the slope retreats to leave a flat plain.

questionText: Minor Tectonic Plates: Scotia (between South America and Antarctica), Caroline (north of New Guinea), Cocos (between Central America and the Pacific), Nazca (South America and the Pacific).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SCNC' (Scotia, Caroline, Nazca, Cocos) as 'Small Crustal Neighborhood Clusters' located near major plate boundaries.

questionText: Lava Types: Basic lava is hot, fluid, iron/magnesium-rich, and forms shields; acid lava is viscous and silica-rich and forms steep cones.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'Basic is Bold' (fluid/low silica) and 'Acid is Angry' (viscous/high silica/explosive).

questionText: Soil Colour: Red soils indicate iron oxides and good drainage; yellow soils have less organic matter and are common in humid regions.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'Red Rust' for iron oxides and 'Yellow Yawn' for the low-energy, low-organic matter humid regions.

questionText: Latitude and Longitude: Latitude measures north-south position, parallels decrease in size toward poles; longitude measures east-west, meridians are semicircles from pole to pole.
mnemonic_hint: Latitude is like a ladder (flat rungs), while Longitude is long lines connecting the poles.

questionText: Atmospheric Layers: Troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone, jet aircraft), mesosphere (meteors burn), thermosphere, exosphere.
mnemonic_hint: To (Troposphere) Strut (Stratosphere) My (Mesosphere) Thermal (Thermosphere) Exit (Exosphere).

questionText: Thunderstorms: Produced by cumulonimbus clouds, they involve updrafts, lightning, thunder, heavy rain, and sometimes hail; short-lived but intense.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'C-U-L-T': Cumulonimbus, Updrafts, Lightning, and Thunder.

questionText: Temperature and Relief: Temperature decreases with altitude (normal lapse rate 6°C/1000 m); mountains are cooler than plains at the same latitude.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'Up-Cool': As you go UP in altitude, the air gets COOL (6 degrees per kilometer).

questionText: Insolation and Terrestrial Radiation: Earth receives shortwave solar energy, radiates longwave energy back; only part of incoming energy reaches the surface, maintaining heat balance.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Short Sun, Long Land': Sun sends shortwaves, Earth sends longwaves back.

questionText: Precipitation Patterns: Rainfall decreases from the equator to the poles; coastal areas get more rain than interiors; equatorial and western temperate regions get year-round rain.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'E-W-C': Equator (wet), West-coasts (wet in temperate), and Continentality (drier interiors).

questionText: Dew Formation: Dew forms on clear, calm, humid, cold nights when surfaces cool below the dew point but above freezing.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CCC' for Dew: Clear skies, Calm winds, and Cold surfaces.

questionText: Temperature Inversion: This occurs on clear, calm nights when the surface cools rapidly, trapping cold air below warmer air. It is common in valleys.
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Cold Blanket'—the cold air gets trapped under the warm air like a blanket on the ground.

questionText: Air Masses: Large bodies of air with uniform temperature and humidity, classified as arctic, polar, or tropical based on origin.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'APT' for Air masses: Arctic (coldest), Polar (cold), Tropical (warm).

questionText: Jet Streams: Narrow bands of strong upper-level winds blow west to east, strongest in winter, transport aerosols and gases.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'JET' as Just Evolving Turbulence—a narrow, fast-moving river of air high in the sky.

questionText: Cyclones: Low-pressure systems with converging winds; tropical cyclones form at the ITCZ, lack fronts, and are energised by convection.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'ITCZ' as the 'Inter-Tropical Cyclone Zone' where warm air rises and fuels the storm.

questionText: Orographic Rainfall: Occurs when moist air rises over mountains, cools, and precipitates on windward slopes; the leeward side is a rain shadow.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Oro' as 'Mountain' (Orography) and 'Windward' as the 'Winning' side that gets all the rain.

questionText: Ocean Currents: Warm currents flow from the equator to the poles, cold from the poles to the equator; the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans have distinct current patterns.
mnemonic_hint: Warm flows from the middle (Equator) to the ends (Poles), while Cold flows from the ends (Poles) to the middle (Equator).

questionText: Tides: Caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and sun and centrifugal force; spring tides (aligned), neap tides (right angle), apogee (moon farthest, low tides).
concepts: Lunar and Solar influence on Earth
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Spring is Straight' (aligned) and 'Neap is Ninety' (right angle).

questionText: Water Vapour: The most important atmospheric gas, decreases with altitude and latitude, lowers air density, and affects pressure.
sub_topic: Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere
concepts: Relationship between humidity and air density
mnemonic_hint: Think of water vapour as 'Heavy-Light': it's heavy for weather but makes air lighter (less dense) because it displaces heavier nitrogen and oxygen molecules.

questionText: Baltic and Dead Sea: Baltic Sea is in Northern Europe, north of the Dead Sea; Dead Sea is a saline lake between Jordan and Israel, on the African-Arabian plate boundary.
sub_topic: World Geography: Major Seas and Lakes
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Baltic is North, Dead is Rift'—the Baltic is near the cold North, while the Dead Sea is trapped in the hot Jordan Rift Valley.

questionText: Thermocline: Ocean layer between 100–400 m depth with rapid temperature decrease; 90% of ocean water is below the thermocline, near 0°C.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Thermo-cline' as a 'Thermal Cliff' where the temperature drops sharply like falling off a ledge.

questionText: Oceanic Landforms: Seamounts (submarine mountains), submarine canyons (deep valleys), atolls (coral islands), guyots (flat-topped seamounts).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-S-A-G': Seamounts (Submarine), Submarine (Canyons), Atolls (Coral), Guyots (G-flat-topped).

questionText: Ocean Temperature Factors: Latitude, prevailing winds, ocean currents, and land-water distribution affect ocean surface temperatures.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-I-L-L': Winds, Insolation (Latitude), Land-water distribution, and Latitudinal currents.

questionText: Ocean Gyres: Large circular current systems driven by wind, Earth’s rotation (Coriolis effect), and landmasses; not directly by tectonic boundaries.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'W-E-L' for Gyres: Wind, Earth's rotation (Coriolis), and Landmasses define the path.

questionText: Salinity and Density: Higher salinity increases seawater density; higher temperature decreases density; cold, saline water sinks, driving thermohaline circulation.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Cold and Salty' as 'Heavy and Sinking' (like a dense rock), while 'Warm' is 'Light and Rising' (like a hot air balloon).

questionText: Hot Deserts: Located on western continental coasts (15°–30°), influenced by trade winds, high pressure, cold currents, and low humidity.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-H-A-T': Western coasts, High pressure, Arid trade winds, and Temperature-lowering cold currents.

questionText: Siberian Climate: Severe continental climate with extreme temperature variation exists in the Northern Hemisphere; absent in the Southern Hemisphere due to lack of large landmasses and ocean moderation.
mnemonic_hint: Siberia is 'Severe' because landmasses are 'S-tretched' wide in the North, while the South is 'S-oaked' by oceans.

questionText: Coniferous Forests: Found in high northern latitudes, dominated by needle-leaved evergreens; soils are acidic, nutrient-poor podzols; trees retain needles for years.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'CONE-iferous' trees as having needles to shed snow, growing in 'POD-zols' (poor, acidic soil) where only the tough survive.

questionText: Shifting Cultivation: Known as Ladang, Taungya, Tamrai, and Humah in Southeast Asia, involves slash-and-burn, short cultivation, and long fallow periods.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'L-T-T-H' for Southeast Asia: Ladang, Taungya, Tamrai, Humah—think of a 'Little Tiny Tropical Harvest'.

questionText: Steppe Climate: Dry grasslands in temperate zones, influenced by westerlies, have extreme seasons in the north, milder in the south, and support short grasses.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'STEP-PE': S-teppe, T-emperate, E-xtreme, P-rairies, P-astures, E-urasia.

questionText: Major Waterways: Panama Canal (Atlantic-Pacific), Suez Canal (Mediterranean-Red Sea), Dardanelles (Aegean-Marmara), English Channel (North Sea-Atlantic).
sub_topic: World Geography: Major Straits and Canals
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Suez-Red' (Red Sea) and 'Panama-Pacific' (Pacific Ocean) as the primary anchors for global trade routes.

questionText: Uranium and Thorium: Both are radioactive metals, never found in pure form; uranium-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope; thorium is more abundant.
mnemonic_hint: Think 'U-235 is the Fissile Star' (U-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope).

questionText: Quinary Activities: Highest-level decision-making and knowledge-based services (executives, scientists, consultants); medical tourism and tourist guides are tertiary, not quinary.
mnemonic_hint: Think of Quinary as the 'Queen's' level—the highest decision-makers who sit at the top of the pyramid.

questionText: Demographic Rates: Fertility rate (births per 1000 women 15–49), infant mortality (deaths under 1 per 1000 live births), maternal mortality (deaths per 100,000 live births), sex ratio (females per 1000 males).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'FIMS': Fertility (1000 women), Infant (1000 births), Maternal (100,000 births), Sex (1000 males).

questionText: Mineral Production: South Africa leads in platinum; China has the largest rare earth reserves; DRC leads in cobalt production; India has significant rare earths but relies on imports.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-C-C-I': Platinum-Cape (South Africa), China-Critical (Rare Earths), Cobalt-Congo (DRC), India-Import (Dependent).

questionText: Migration Factors: Push factors include disasters, political instability, and lack of services; pull factors include better jobs and opportunities.
mnemonic_hint: Push away from problems (disasters/instability), Pull towards potential (jobs/opportunities).

questionText: Disputed Regions: Essequibo (Guyana/Venezuela), Abyei (Sudan/South Sudan), Tigray (Ethiopia), Socotra (Yemen).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'EATS': Essequibo (Guyana), Abyei (Sudan), Tigray (Ethiopia), Socotra (Yemen).

questionText: Footloose Industries: Can locate anywhere, require little labour, not tied to resources; examples include diamond cutting and electronics.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Footloose' as having 'feet' that can walk anywhere because they aren't chained to heavy raw materials.

questionText: Southeast Asian Cities (South to North): Phnom Penh (Cambodia), Bangkok (Thailand), Vientiane (Laos), Hanoi (Vietnam).
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'PBVH' (Phnom, Bangkok, Vientiane, Hanoi) as 'Please Bring Very Hot' tea, moving from the southern tropical plains up to the northern capital.

questionText: Eastern Maritime Corridor: Chennai-Vladivostok sea route connects India and Russia, reducing transit time and distance, passing through key Asian ports.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'C-V' as 'Chennai-Vladivostok', the Cold-to-Warm corridor connecting the Bay of Bengal to the Sea of Japan.

questionText: Major Rivers and Cities: Danube (Vienna), Yangtze (Shanghai), Seine (Paris); Brasília is not on the Rio de la Plata.
sub_topic: World Geography: Rivers and Associated Cities
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'VDS' (Vienna-Danube, Seine-Paris) and note that Brasília is inland, not on a major river estuary.

questionText: British-Type Climate: Cool temperate western margins, influenced by westerlies, cyclonic activity, and deciduous forests with seasonal leaf fall.
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'B-W-C': British-type, Western-margin, Cyclonic-activity.

questionText: Largest Landlocked Countries: Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Chad, Niger, Mali, and Ethiopia are the world’s largest landlocked nations.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'K-M-C-N-M-E' (Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Chad, Niger, Mali, Ethiopia) as 'Keep My Cold Night More Energetic'.

questionText: Mediterranean Climate: Found on western continental coasts (30°–40°), with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters; supports crops like grapes and olives.
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'MED-W-O' (Mediterranean, West coast, Olives/Orchards) for the climate's location and signature crops.

questionText: Horn of Africa: Includes Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia; bordered by the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Indian Ocean; Kenya is not part of the Horn.
sub_topic: Geopolitics of the Horn of Africa
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SEED': Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Djibouti.
